'''Whitehead's algorithm''' is a mathematical algorithm in [[group theory]] for solving the automorphic equivalence problem in the finite rank [[free group]] ''F<sub>n</sub>''. The algorithm is based on a classic 1936 paper of [[J. H. C. Whitehead]].<ref name=Wh>[[J. H. C. Whitehead]], ''On equivalent sets of elements in a free group'', [[Annals of Mathematics|Ann. of Math. (2)]] 37:4 (1936), 782–800. {{MR|1503309}}</ref> It is still unknown (except for the case ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2) if Whitehead's algorithm has [[P (complexity)|polynomial time complexity]].

==Statement of the problem==

Let <math> F_n=F(x_1,\dots, x_n)</math> be a free group of rank <math>n\ge 2</math> with a free basis <math> X=\{x_1,\dots, x_n\}</math>. The '''automorphism problem''', or the '''automorphic equivalence problem''' for <math>F_n</math> asks, given two freely reduced words <math> w, w'\in F_n</math> whether there exists an [[Automorphism group of a free group|automorphism]] <math>\varphi\in \operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that <math> \varphi(w)=w'</math>.

Thus the automorphism problem asks, for <math> w, w'\in F_n</math> whether <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math>.
For <math> w, w'\in F_n</math> one has <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math> if and only if <math>\operatorname{Out}(F_n)[w]=\operatorname{Out}(F_n)[w']</math>, where <math>[w], [w']</math> are [[conjugacy class]]es in <math>F_n</math> of <math> w, w'</math> accordingly. Therefore, the automorphism problem for <math>F_n</math> is often formulated in terms of <math>\operatorname{Out}(F_n)</math>-equivalence of conjugacy classes of elements of <math>F_n</math>.

For an element <math> w\in F_n</math>, <math>|w|_X</math> denotes the freely reduced length of <math>w</math> with respect to <math>X</math>, and <math>\|w\|_X</math> denotes the cyclically reduced length of <math>w</math> with respect to <math>X</math>. For the automorphism problem, the length of an input <math>w</math> is measured as <math>|w|_X</math> or as <math>\|w\|_X</math>, depending on whether one views <math>w</math> as an element of <math>F_n</math> or as defining the corresponding conjugacy class <math>[w]</math> in <math>F_n</math>.

==History==

The automorphism problem for <math>F_n</math> was algorithmically solved by [[J. H. C. Whitehead]] in a classic 1936 paper,<ref name=Wh/> and his solution came to be known as Whitehead's algorithm. Whitehead used a topological approach in his paper. Namely, consider the 3-manifold <math>M_n=\#_{i=1}^n \mathbb S^2\times \mathbb S^1</math>, the [[connected sum]] of <math>n</math> copies of <math>\mathbb S^2\times \mathbb S^1</math>. Then <math>\pi_1(M_n)\cong F_n</math>, and, moreover, up to a quotient by a finite [[normal subgroup]] isomorphic to <math>\mathbb Z_2^n</math>, the [[mapping class group]] of <math>M_n</math> is equal to <math>\operatorname{Out}(F_n)</math>; see.<ref>Suhas Pandit, ''A note on automorphisms of the sphere complex.'' Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. Math. Sci. 124:2 (2014), 255–265; {{MR|3218895}}</ref> Different free bases of <math>F_n</math> can be represented by isotopy classes of "sphere systems" in <math>M_n</math>, and the cyclically reduced form of an element <math>w\in F_n</math>, as well as the Whitehead graph of <math>[w]</math>, can be "read-off" from how a loop in [[general position]] representing  <math>[w]</math> intersects the spheres in the system.  Whitehead moves can be represented by certain kinds of topological "swapping" moves modifying the sphere system.<ref>[[Allen Hatcher]], ''Homological stability for automorphism groups of free groups'', [[Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici]] 70:1 (1995) 39–62; {{MR|1314940}}</ref><ref>[[Karen Vogtmann]], ''Automorphisms of free groups and outer space.''
Proceedings of the Conference on Geometric and Combinatorial Group Theory, Part I (Haifa, 2000). 
[[Geometriae Dedicata]] '''94''' (2002), 1–31; {{MR|1950871}}</ref><ref>Andrew Clifford, and Richard Z. Goldstein, ''Sets of primitive elements in a free group.'' 
[[Journal of Algebra]] '''357''' (2012), 271–278; {{MR|2905255}}</ref>

Subsequently, Rapaport,<ref>Elvira Rapaport, ''On free groups and their automorphisms''. 
[[Acta Mathematica]] '''99''' (1958), 139–163; {{MR|0131452}}</ref> and later, based on her work, Higgins and [[Roger Lyndon|Lyndon]],<ref>P. J. Higgins, and R. C. Lyndon, ''Equivalence of elements under automorphisms of a free group.'' 
[[Journal of the London Mathematical Society|Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2)]] '''8''' (1974), 254–258; {{MR|0340420}}</ref> gave a purely combinatorial and algebraic re-interpretation of Whitehead's work and of Whitehead's algorithm. The exposition of Whitehead's algorithm in the book of Lyndon and [[Paul Schupp|Schupp]]<ref name=LS/> is based on this combinatorial approach. [[Marc Culler|Culler]] and [[Karen Vogtmann|Vogtmann]],<ref name=CV/> in their 1986 paper that introduced the [[Outer space (mathematics)|Outer space]], gave a hybrid approach to Whitehead's algorithm, presented in combinatorial terms but closely following Whitehead's original ideas.

==Whitehead's algorithm==

Our exposition regarding Whitehead's algorithm mostly follows Ch.I.4 in the book of [[Roger Lyndon|Lyndon]] and [[Paul Schupp|Schupp]],<ref name=LS>[[Roger Lyndon]] and [[Paul Schupp]], [https://books.google.com/books?id=aiPVBygHi_oC&q=lyndon+and+schupp ''Combinatorial group theory''.] Reprint of the 1977 edition. Classics in Mathematics. [[Springer-Verlag]], Berlin, 2001. {{isbn|3-540-41158-5}}{{MR|1812024}}</ref> as well as.<ref name=KSS/>

===Overview===

The [[Automorphism group of a free group|automorphism group]] <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> has a particularly useful finite generating set <math> \mathcal W</math> of '''Whitehead automorphisms''' or '''Whitehead moves'''.  Given <math>w,w'\in F_n </math> the first part of Whitehead's algorithm consists of iteratively applying Whitehead moves to <math>w,w'</math> to take each of them to an "automorphically minimal" form, where the cyclically reduced length strictly decreases at each step. Once we find automorphically these minimal forms <math>u,u'</math> of <math>w,w'</math>, we check if <math>\|u\|_X=\|u'\|_X</math>.  If <math>\|u\|_X\ne \|u'\|_X</math> then <math>w,w'</math> are not automorphically equivalent in <math>F_n</math>.

If <math>\|u\|_X=\|u'\|_X</math>, we check if there exists a finite chain of Whitehead moves taking <math>u</math> to <math>u'</math> so that the cyclically reduced length remains constant throughout this chain. The elements <math>w,w'</math> are not automorphically equivalent in <math>F_n</math> [[if and only if]] such a chain exists.

Whitehead's algorithm also solves the ''search automorphism problem'' for <math>F_n</math>. Namely, given <math>w,w'\in F_n </math>, if Whitehead's algorithm concludes that <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math>, the algorithm also outputs an automorphism <math>\varphi\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that <math>\varphi(w)=w'</math>. Such an element <math>\varphi\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> is produced as the composition of a chain of Whitehead moves arising from the above procedure and taking <math>w</math> to <math>w'</math>.

===Whitehead automorphisms===

A '''Whitehead automorphism''', or '''Whitehead move''', of <math>F_n</math> is an automorphism <math>\tau\in \operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> of <math>F_n</math> of one of the following two types:

# There is a permutation <math>\sigma\in S_n</math> of <math>\{1,2,\dots, n\}</math> such that for <math>i=1,\dots, n</math> <math display=block> \tau(x_i)=x_{\sigma(i)}^{\pm 1}</math> Such <math>\tau</math> is called a '''Whitehead automorphism of the first kind'''.
#  There is an element <math>a\in X^{\pm 1}</math>, called the '''multiplier''', such that for every <math>x\in X^{\pm 1}</math> <math display=block>\tau(x)\in \{x, xa, a^{-1}x, a^{-1}xa\}.</math> Such <math>\tau</math> is called a '''Whitehead automorphism of the second kind'''. Since <math>\tau</math> is an automorphism of <math>F_n</math>, it follows that <math>\tau(a)=a</math> in this case.

Often, for a Whitehead automorphism <math>\tau\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math>, the corresponding [[outer automorphism]] in [[Out(Fn)|<math>\operatorname{Out}(F_n)</math>]] is also called a Whitehead automorphism or a Whitehead move.
   
====Examples====
Let <math>F_4=F(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)</math>.

Let <math>\tau: F_4\to F_4</math> be a homomorphism such that
<math display=block> \tau(x_1)=x_2x_1, \quad \tau(x_2)=x_2, \quad\tau(x_3)=x_2x_3x_2^{-1},\quad \tau(x_4)=x_4</math>
Then <math>\tau</math> is actually an automorphism of <math>F_4</math>, and, moreover, <math>\tau</math> is a Whitehead automorphism of the second kind, with the multiplier <math>a=x_2^{-1}</math>.

Let <math>\tau': F_4\to F_4</math> be a homomorphism such that
<math display=block> \tau'(x_1)=x_1, \quad \tau'(x_2)=x_1^{-1}x_2x_1, \quad\tau'(x_3)=x_1^{-1}x_3x_1,\quad \tau'(x_4)=x_1^{-1}x_4x_1</math>
Then <math>\tau'</math> is actually an [[inner automorphism]] of <math>F_4</math> given by conjugation by <math>x_1</math>, and, moreover, <math>\tau'</math> is a Whitehead automorphism of the second kind, with the multiplier <math>a=x_1</math>.

===Automorphically minimal and Whitehead minimal elements===

For <math>w\in F_n</math>, the conjugacy class <math>[w]</math> is called '''automorphically minimal''' if for every <math>\varphi\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> we have <math>\|w\|_X\le \|\varphi(w)\|_X</math>. 
Also, a conjugacy class <math>[w]</math> is called '''Whitehead minimal''' if for every Whitehead move <math>\tau\in \operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> we have <math>\|w\|_X\le \|\tau(w)\|_X</math>.

Thus, by definition, if <math>[w]</math> is automorphically minimal then it is also Whitehead minimal. It turns out that the converse is also true.

===Whitehead's "Peak Reduction Lemma"===

The following statement is referred to as Whitehead's "Peak Reduction Lemma", see Proposition 4.20 in <ref name=LS/> and Proposition 1.2 in:<ref name=KSS>Ilya Kapovich, Paul Schupp, and Vladimir Shpilrain, ''Generic properties of Whitehead's algorithm and isomorphism rigidity of random one-relator groups.'' [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] 223:1 (2006), 113–140</ref>

Let <math>w\in F_n</math>. Then the following hold:

# If <math>[w]</math> is not automorphically minimal, then there exists a Whitehead automorphism <math>\tau\in \operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that  <math>\|\tau(w)\|_X< \|w\|_X</math>.

#Suppose that <math>[w]</math> is automorphically minimal, and that another conjugacy class <math>[w']</math> is also automorphically minimal. Then <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math> if and only if <math>\|w\|_X=\|w'\|_X</math> and there exists a finite sequence of Whitehead moves <math>\tau_1,\dots, \tau_k\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that <math display=block>\tau_k\cdots \tau_1(w)=w'</math> and <math display=block> \|\tau_i\cdots\tau_1(w)\|_X=\|w\|_X \text{ for } i=1,\dots, k.</math>

Part (1) of the Peak Reduction Lemma implies that a conjugacy class <math>[w]</math> is Whitehead minimal if and only if it is automorphically minimal.

===The automorphism graph===

The '''automorphism graph''' <math>\mathcal A</math> of <math>F_n</math> is a graph with the vertex set being the set of conjugacy classes <math>[u]</math> of elements <math>u\in F_n</math>. Two distinct vertices <math>[u], [v]</math> are adjacent in <math>\mathcal A</math> if <math>\|u\|_X=\|v\|_X</math> and there exists a Whitehead automorphism <math>\tau</math> such that <math>[\tau(u)]=[v]</math>. For a vertex <math>[u]</math> of <math>\mathcal A</math>, the connected component of <math>[u]</math> in <math>\mathcal A</math> is denoted <math>\mathcal A[u]</math>.

===Whitehead graph===

For <math>1\ne w\in F_n</math> with cyclically reduced form <math>u</math>, the '''Whitehead graph''' <math>\Gamma_{[w]}</math> is a labelled graph with the vertex set <math>X^{\pm 1}</math>, where for <math>x,y\in X^{\pm 1}, x\ne y</math> there is an edge joining <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> with the label or "weight" <math>n(\{x,y\};[w])</math> which is equal to the number of distinct occurrences of subwords <math>x^{-1}y, y^{-1}x</math> read cyclically in <math>u</math>. (In some versions of the Whitehead graph one only includes the edges with <math>n(\{x,y\};[w])>0</math>.)

If <math>\tau\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> is a Whitehead automorphism, then the length change <math>\|\tau(w)\|_X-\|w\|_X</math> can be expressed as a [[linear combination]], with [[integer]] coefficients determined by <math>\tau</math>, of the weights <math>n(\{x,y\};[w])</math> in the Whitehead graph <math>\Gamma_{[w]}</math>. See Proposition 4.16 in Ch. I of.<ref name=LS/> This fact plays a key role in the proof of Whitehead's peak reduction result.

===Whitehead's minimization algorithm===

'''Whitehead's minimization algorithm''', given a freely reduced word <math>w\in F_n</math>, finds an automorphically minimal <math>[v]</math> such that <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)v.</math>

This algorithm proceeds as follows.  Given <math>w\in F_n</math>, put <math>w_1=w</math>. If <math>w_i</math> is already constructed, check if there exists a Whitehead automorphism <math>\tau\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that <math>\|\tau(w_i)\|_X<\|w_i\|_X</math>. (This condition can be checked since the set of Whitehead automorphisms of <math>F_n</math> is finite.) If such <math>\tau</math> exists, put <math>w_{i+1}=\tau(w_i)</math> and go to the next step. If no such <math>\tau</math> exists, declare that <math>[w_i]</math> is automorphically minimal, with <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w_i</math>, and terminate the algorithm.

Part (1) of the Peak Reduction Lemma implies that the Whitehead's minimization algorithm terminates with some <math>w_m</math>, where <math>m\le\|w\|_X</math>, and that then <math>[w_m]</math> is indeed automorphically minimal and satisfies <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w_m</math>.

===Whitehead's algorithm for the automorphic equivalence problem===

'''Whitehead's algorithm''' for the automorphic equivalence problem, given <math>w,w'\in F_n</math> decides whether or not <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math>.

The algorithm proceeds as follows. Given <math>w,w'\in F_n</math>, first apply the Whitehead minimization algorithm to each of <math>w,w'</math> to find automorphically minimal <math>[v],[v']</math> such that <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)v</math> and <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)v'</math>.  If <math>\|v\|_X\ne \|v'\|_X</math>, declare that <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w\ne\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math> and terminate the algorithm. Suppose now that <math>\|v\|_X=\|v'\|_X=t\ge 0</math>. Then check if there exists a 
finite sequence of Whitehead moves <math>\tau_1,\dots, \tau_k\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that <math display=block>\tau_k\dots \tau_1(v)=v'</math> and <math display=block> \|\tau_i\dots\tau_1(v)\|_X=\|v\|_X=t \text{ for } i=1,\dots, k.</math>

This condition can be checked since the number of cyclically reduced words of length <math>t</math> in <math>F_n</math> is finite. More specifically, using the [[breadth-first search|breadth-first approach]], one constructs the connected components <math>\mathcal A[v], \mathcal A[v']</math> of the automorphism graph and checks if <math>\mathcal A[v]\cap \mathcal A[v']=\varnothing</math>.

If such a sequence exists, declare that <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math>, and terminate the algorithm. If no such sequence exists, declare that <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w\neq\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math> and terminate the algorithm.

The Peak Reduction Lemma implies that Whitehead's algorithm correctly solves the automorphic equivalence problem in <math> F_n</math>. Moreover, if <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math>, the algorithm actually produces (as a composition of Whitehead moves) an automorphism <math>\varphi\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that <math>\varphi(w)=w'</math>.

==Computational complexity of Whitehead's algorithm==
{{unsolved|mathematics|What is the worst-case asymptotic time complexity of Whithead's algorithm?}}
A priori, the [[Worst-case complexity|worst-case]] asymptotic [[time complexity]] of Whitehead's algorithm may be [[EXPTIME|exponential]] in terms of the size of an input word. Whether that bound is achieved is unknown.<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = De Gruyter| isbn = 9783119146791 | last1 = Kapovich| first1 = Ilya| last2 = Myasnikov| first2 = Alexei| last3 = Shpilrain| first3 = Vladimir| title = Combinatorial group theory: Open problems on infinite groups| access-date = 2026-03-05| date = 2026-03-16| url = https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783112208137/html | pages = 12-13}}</ref> There are several partial results showing stronger bounds on aspects of the algorithm.

* Whitehead's minimization algorithm runs in [[polynomial time]] for a fixed rank of free group. If the rank <math>n\ge 2</math> of <math>F_n</math> is fixed, then, given <math>w\in F_n</math>, the Whitehead minimization algorithm always terminates in quadratic time <math>O(|w|_X^2)</math> and produces an automorphically minimal word in the automorphic orbit of <math>w</math>.<ref name=KSS/> Moreover, even if <math>n</math> is not considered fixed, (an adaptation of) the Whitehead minimization algorithm on an input <math>w\in F_n</math> terminates in time <math>O(|w|_X^2 n^3)</math>.<ref>Abdó Roig, Enric Ventura, and Pascal Weil, ''On the complexity of the Whitehead minimization problem.'' [[International Journal of Algebra and Computation]] 17:8 (2007), 1611–1634; {{MR|2378055}}</ref>
* If the rank <math>n\ge 3</math> of <math>F_n</math> is fixed, then for an automorphically minimal <math>u\in F_n</math> constructing the graph <math>\mathcal A[u]</math> takes <math>O\left(\|u\|_X\cdot \#V\mathcal A[u]\right)</math> time and thus requires a priori exponential time in <math>|u|_X</math>. For that reason Whitehead's algorithm for deciding, given <math>w,w'\in F_n</math>, whether or not <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w=\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)w'</math>, runs in at most exponential time in <math>\max\{|w|_X,|w'|_X\}</math>.
* For <math>n=2</math>, Khan proved that for an automorphically minimal <math>u\in F_2</math>, the graph <math>\mathcal A[u]</math> has at most <math>O\left(\|u\|_X\right)</math> vertices and hence  constructing the graph <math>\mathcal A[u]</math> can be done in quadratic time in <math>|u|_X</math>.<ref name=Kh>Bilal Khan, 
''The structure of automorphic conjugacy in the free group of rank two''.  Computational and experimental group theory, 115–196, 
Contemp. Math., 349, [[American Mathematical Society]], Providence, RI, 2004</ref> Consequently, Whitehead's algorithm for the automorphic equivalence problem in <math>F_2</math>, given <math>w,w'\in F_2</math> runs in quadratic time in <math>\max\{|w|_X,|w'|_X\}</math>.
* For fixed <math>n\geq 2</math>, Lee proved that for automorphically minimal <math>u\in F_n</math> in which the number of times each generator appears (either with positive or negative exponent) is unique, the size of <math>\mathcal A[u]</math> is <math>O\left(|u|^{n(5n-7)/2}\right)</math>, a polynomial with respect to the length of <math>u</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.jalgebra.2006.04.012| issn = 00218693| volume = 301| issue = 1| pages = 35–58| last = Lee| first = Donghi| title = Counting words of minimum length in an automorphic orbit| journal = Journal of Algebra| access-date = 2025-08-27| date = 2006| url = https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021869306002043| url-access = subscription}}</ref> The set of words for which this applies is [[Generic property|generic]] in <math>F_n</math>.<ref name="AverageCase">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1080/00927872.2022.2113791| issn = 0092-7872| volume = 51| issue = 2| pages = 799–806| last = Shpilrain| first = Vladimir| title = Average-case complexity of the Whitehead problem for free groups| journal = Communications in Algebra| access-date = 2025-07-15| date = 2023-02-01| url = https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00927872.2022.2113791| url-access = subscription}}</ref>

The [[average-case]] time complexity of Whitehead's algorithm is also unknown. For a fixed rank of free group, if <math>\mathcal A[u]</math> is bounded by a polynomial, then the average time complexity is linear.<ref name="AverageCase"/> Thus it is linear when restricted to <math>F_2</math>.<ref name="AverageCase"/>

==Applications, generalizations and related results==

*Whitehead's algorithm can be adapted to solve, for any fixed <math>m\ge 1</math>, the automorphic equivalence problem for ''m''-tuples of elects of <math>F_n</math> and for ''m''-tuples of conjugacy classes in <math>F_n</math>; see Ch.I.4 of <ref name=LS/> and <ref>Sava Krstić, Martin Lustig, and [[Karen Vogtmann]], ''An equivariant Whitehead algorithm and conjugacy for roots of Dehn twist automorphisms''. [[Proceedings of the Edinburgh Mathematical Society|Proceedings of the Edinburgh Mathematical Society (2)]] 44:1 (2001), 117–141</ref>
*McCool used Whitehead's algorithm and the peak reduction to prove that for any <math>w\in F_n</math> the stabilizer <math> \operatorname{Stab}_{\operatorname{Out}(F_n)}([w])</math> is [[finitely presented group|finitely presentable]], and obtained a similar results for <math>\operatorname{Out}(F_n)</math>-stabilizers of ''m''-tuples of conjugacy classes in <math>F_n</math>.<ref>James McCool, ''Some finitely presented subgroups of the automorphism group of a free group.'' [[Journal of Algebra]] 35:1-3 (1975), 205–213; {{MR|0396764}}</ref> McCool also used the peak reduction method to construct of a finite presentation of the group <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> with the set of Whitehead automorphisms as the generating set.<ref>James McCool, ''A presentation for the automorphism group of a free group of finite rank.'' [[Journal of the London Mathematical Society|Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2)]] '''8''' (1974), 259–266; {{MR|0340421}}</ref> He then used this presentation to recover a finite presentation for <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math>, originally due to [[Jakob Nielsen (mathematician)|Nielsen]], with Nielsen automorphisms as generators.<ref>James McCool, ''On Nielsen's presentation of the automorphism group of a free group''. [[Journal of the London Mathematical Society|Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2)]] '''10''' (1975), 265–270</ref>
*Gersten obtained a variation of Whitehead's algorithm, for deciding, given two finite subsets <math> S,S'\subseteq F_n</math>, whether the [[subgroup]]s <math>H=\langle S\rangle, H'=\langle S'\rangle\le F_n</math> are automorphically equivalent, that is, whether there exists <math>\varphi\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math> such that <math>\varphi(H)=H'</math>.<ref>Stephen Gersten, ''On Whitehead's algorithm'', [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] 10:2 (1984), 281–284; {{MR|0733696}}</ref>
*Whitehead's algorithm and peak reduction play a key role in the proof by [[Marc Culler|Culler]] and [[Karen Vogtmann|Vogtmann]] that the [[Outer space (mathematics)|Culler–Vogtmann Outer space]] is [[Contractible space|contractible]].<ref name=CV>{{cite journal | author1 = [[Marc Culler]]  |author2=[[Karen Vogtmann]]  | title = Moduli of graphs and automorphisms of free groups | journal = Inventiones Mathematicae | volume = 84 | issue = 1 | pages = 91–119 | year=1986 | url=https://www.math.cornell.edu/~vogtmann/ScannedPapers/1986.0084.pdf | doi = 10.1007/BF01388734|mr=0830040|s2cid=122869546 }}</ref>
*Collins and [[Heiner Zieschang|Zieschang]] obtained analogs of Whitehead's peak reduction and of Whitehead's algorithm for automorphic equivalence in [[free product]]s of groups.<ref>Donald J. Collins, and [[Heiner Zieschang]], 
''Rescuing the Whitehead method for free products. I. Peak reduction.''  [[Mathematische Zeitschrift]] 185:4 (1984), 487–504 {{MR|0733769}}</ref><ref>Donald J. Collins, and [[Heiner Zieschang]], 
''Rescuing the Whitehead method for free products. II. The algorithm.''  [[Mathematische Zeitschrift]] 186:3 (1984), 335–361; {{MR|0744825}}</ref>
*Gilbert used a version of a peak reduction lemma to construct a presentation for the [[automorphism group]] <math>\operatorname{Aut}(G)</math> of a [[free product]] <math>G=\ast_{i=1}^m G_i</math>.<ref>Nick D. Gilbert, ''Presentations of the automorphism group of a free product''. [[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]] (3) '''54''' (1987), no. 1, 115–140.</ref>
*Levitt and [[Karen Vogtmann|Vogtmann]] produced a Whitehead-type algorithm for solving the automorphic equivalence problem (for elects, ''m''-tuples of elements and ''m''-tuples of conjugacy classes) in a group <math>G=\pi_1(S)</math> where <math>S</math> is a closed hyperbolic surface.<ref>Gilbert Levitt and [[Karen Vogtmann]], ''A Whitehead algorithm for surface groups'', [[Topology (journal)|Topology]] 39:6 (2000), 1239–1251</ref>
*If an element <math>w\in F_n=F(X)</math> chosen uniformly at random from the sphere of radius <math>m\ge 1</math> in  <math>F(X)</math>, then, with probability tending to ''1'' exponentially fast as <math>m\to\infty</math>, the conjugacy class <math>[w]</math> is already automorphically minimal and, moreover, <math>\#V\mathcal A[w]=O\left(\|w\|_X\right)=O(m)</math>. Consequently, if <math>w,w'\in F_n</math> are two such ``generic" elements, Whitehead's algorithm decides whether <math>w,w'</math> are automorphically equivalent in linear time in <math>\max\{|w|_X,|w'|_X\}</math>.<ref name=KSS/>
*Similar to the above results hold for the [[generic-case complexity|genericity]] of automorphic minimality for ``randomly chosen" finitely generated subgroups of <math>F_n</math>.<ref>Frédérique Bassino, Cyril Nicaud, and Pascal Weil, ''On the genericity of Whitehead minimality''.  [[Journal of Group Theory]] 19:1 (2016), 137–159 {{MR|3441131}}</ref>
*Lee proved that if <math>u\in F_n=F(X)</math> is a cyclically reduced word such that <math>[u]</math> is automorphically minimal, and if whenever <math>x_i,x_j, i<j</math> both occur in <math>u</math> or <math>u^{-1}</math> then the total number of occurrences of <math>x_i^{\pm 1}</math> in <math>u</math> is smaller than the number of occurrences of <math>x_i^{\pm 1}</math>, then <math>\#V\mathcal A[u]</math> is bounded above by a polynomial of degree <math>2n-3</math> in <math>|u|_X</math>.<ref>Donghi Lee, ''A tighter bound for the number of words of minimum length in an automorphic orbit''. [[Journal of Algebra]] 305:2 (2006), 1093–1101; {{MR|2266870}}</ref> Consequently, if <math>w,w'\in F_n, n\ge 3</math> are such that <math>w</math> is automorphically equivalent to some <math>u</math> with the above property, then Whitehead's algorithm decides whether <math>w,w'</math> are automorphically equivalent in time <math>O\left(\max\{|w|_X^{2n-3},|w'|_X^2\}\right)</math>.
*The [[Garside element|Garside algorithm]] for solving the [[conjugacy problem]] in [[braid group]]s has a similar general structure to Whitehead's algorithm, with "cycling moves" playing the role of Whitehead moves.<ref>[[Joan Birman]], Ki Hyoung Ko, and Sang Jin Lee, ''A new approach to the word and conjugacy problems in the braid groups'', [[Advances in Mathematics]] 139:2 (1998), 322–353; {{Zbl|0937.20016}} {{MR|1654165}}</ref>
*Clifford and Goldstein used Whitehead-algorithm based techniques to produce an algorithm that, given a finite subset <math>Z\subseteq F_n</math> decides whether or not the subgroup <math>H=\langle Z\rangle\le F_n</math> contains a '''{{vanchor| primitive element}}''' of <math>F_n,</math> that is an element of a free generating set of <math>F_n.</math><ref>Andrew Clifford, and Richard Z. Goldstein, ''Subgroups of free groups and primitive elements.'' [[Journal of Group Theory]] 13:4 (2010), 601–611;  {{MR|2661660}}</ref>
*Day obtained analogs of Whitehead's algorithm and of Whitehead's peak reduction for automorphic equivalence of elements of [[right-angled Artin group]]s.<ref>Matthew Day, ''Full-featured peak reduction in right-angled Artin groups''. [[Algebraic and Geometric Topology]] 14:3 (2014), 1677–1743 {{MR|3212581}}</ref>
